0.title: Leading a Business for Christ
0.essay:
Most Christians spend most of their waking hours at work, and many lead a team, a firm or a company. This study asks what it means to build and lead a business under the lordship of Christ: how to treat employees, customers, suppliers and competitors, and how to handle profit, power and failure.

Who it is for

It is written for owners, founders, directors and managers, from the person running a one-van plumbing business to the chief executive of a large company. Much of it applies to anyone who leads people at work. It builds on the study Christian at Work, which deals with vocation in general.

The big idea

A business is not a neutral machine for making money, with Christianity added on Sundays. Nor is it merely a platform for evangelism. It is a way of serving God and neighbour by creating goods and services people need, providing work, and dealing honestly in the marketplace. “Whatever you do, work heartily, as for the Lord and not for men” (Colossians 3:23). A company can show the character of God in a thousand ordinary decisions.

The chapters

1. Why Business Matters to God: creation, service and profit. 2. The Leader’s Heart: stewardship, humility and integrity. 3. Employees: wages, culture, hiring and firing. 4. Customers: honest products, prices and promises. 5. Suppliers and Partners: contracts, payment and supply chains. 6. Competitors, Government and Money: fair competition, tax, debt and generosity. 7. Hard Decisions, Failure and Success.

For reflection

If someone watched your business for a month without hearing you speak, what would they conclude about the God you serve?

1.title: Why Business Matters to God
1.essay:
God is a worker, and he made people to work. Business, rightly done, is part of the calling to fill the earth and make something of it. It is not a lesser activity than church work.

The creation mandate

God told the first humans, “Be fruitful and multiply and fill the earth and subdue it” (Genesis 1:28). He put Adam in the garden “to work it and keep it” (Genesis 2:15). Before there was any sin, there was work. Turning raw materials into useful things, organising people to do together what none could do alone, and bringing goods to those who need them: these are ways of taking up that mandate. A baker, a software company and a builder’s firm all serve the world God made.

Business as service

At its best, a business serves people. It meets real needs: food, shelter, transport, health, information, beauty. It provides jobs, so that families can be fed and people can use their gifts. Jesus said, “whoever would be great among you must be your servant” (Mark 10:43). That is true in a company too. A business exists for its customers, its workers and its community, not only for its owners.

What about profit?

Profit is not dirty. It is a sign that a business is creating more value than it uses up, and it allows the business to survive, grow, pay its people and give. The parable of the talents praises the servants who traded and gained more (Matthew 25:16–17). And “it is he who gives you power to get wealth” (Deuteronomy 8:18).

But profit is not the goal. It is like food for a body: necessary, but not the reason to live. When profit becomes the goal, people become tools, and honesty becomes negotiable. “For the love of money is a root of all kinds of evils” (1 Timothy 6:10). The question is not whether to make a profit, but how, and what for.

Two errors

Some Christians treat business as a secular thing, a necessary evil to fund the real work of the church. That is the old split between sacred and secular that the Reformers rejected. Luther said the maid who sweeps the floor serves God as truly as the monk. Others treat business as merely a means for evangelism, valuing it only for the chance to share the gospel. Evangelism matters, but the work itself also matters to God. A good product, honestly made, is pleasing to him.

Your company under Christ

Abraham Kuyper said there is not a square inch of human existence over which Christ does not say, “Mine!” That includes the boardroom, the warehouse and the balance sheet. The Christian business leader does not own the business in the final sense. They manage it for its real owner. “The earth is the LORD’s and the fullness thereof” (Psalm 24:1).

A Tuesday afternoon

Imagine a small engineering firm. The owner looks at a new order and asks three questions: Will it meet a real need? Can we do it well and honestly? Will it be good for our people? He is not doing anything unusual, but he is doing it before God. That is what Christian business looks like most of the time.

For reflection

Do you see your business, or your work, as a way of serving God and your neighbour, or only as a way of making money?

2.title: The Leader’s Heart
2.essay:
A business takes on the character of its leader. Before strategy, structure or culture, there is the heart of the person at the top. The Christian leader leads as a steward, a servant and a person of integrity.

A steward, not an owner

Whatever the shareholding says, you are a steward. You will give account to God for how you used the money, the people and the influence he gave you. “Moreover, it is required of stewards that they be found faithful” (1 Corinthians 4:2). This frees you from the illusion of control, and it holds you to a higher standard than the law or the market.

A servant

Jesus contrasted two kinds of leaders: “You know that those who are considered rulers of the Gentiles lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. But it shall not be so among you” (Mark 10:42–43). Servant leadership does not mean weak leadership. Jesus was decisive, demanding and clear. But he used his power for others. A servant leader makes decisions for the good of the people and the mission, not to feed their own ego.

Integrity

“Whoever walks in integrity walks securely, but he who makes his ways crooked will be found out” (Proverbs 10:9). Integrity means being the same person in every setting: in the board meeting and the pub, in the sales pitch and the tax return. It means keeping your word. It means not using a little dishonesty to win, even when everyone else does. Daniel’s enemies could “find no ground for complaint or any fault, because he was faithful, and no error or fault was found in him” (Daniel 6:4).

Ambition

Is ambition wrong? Not in itself. Paul made it his “ambition to preach the gospel, not where Christ has already been named” (Romans 15:20). Ambition to build something good, to serve more people, or to provide more jobs can be godly. But ambition easily turns into pride or greed. Ask whose glory you are seeking. “Do nothing from selfish ambition or conceit, but in humility count others more significant than yourselves” (Philippians 2:3).

Humility

Proud leaders do not listen. They surround themselves with people who agree, and they cannot admit mistakes. Humble leaders seek counsel, give credit away and own their failures. “Where there is no guidance, a people falls, but in an abundance of counselors there is safety” (Proverbs 11:14). Build a board or a circle of advisers who will tell you the truth, including at least one wise Christian who will ask about your soul.

Rest and family

Many business leaders sacrifice their health, marriage and children on the altar of the company. But a Sabbath rhythm is a confession that the world does not depend on you. God rested, and he commands rest. Psalm 127 warns: “It is in vain that you rise up early and go late to rest, eating the bread of anxious toil; for he gives to his beloved sleep” (Psalm 127:2). Your first ministry is to your family. No business success will make up for losing them.

A Tuesday afternoon

A managing director realises that the figures she presented to the bank last week were too optimistic. Nobody else has noticed. She rings the bank, explains the correction, and takes the embarrassment. It costs her a little pride and possibly a better rate. It gains her a clear conscience, and over time, a reputation that money cannot buy.

For reflection

Who in your life has permission to tell you the truth about your leadership and your heart?

3.title: Employees
3.essay:
Your employees are not resources. They are people made in the image of God, and you will give account for how you treated them. “Masters, treat your bondservants justly and fairly, knowing that you also have a Master in heaven” (Colossians 4:1).

The image of God

The modern phrase “human resources” can hide the truth. A worker is not a cost to be minimised, but a person with a soul, a family and a calling. They will outlast your company; they will live for ever. This does not mean you cannot manage them firmly or let them go. But it shapes how you do everything.

Fair pay

Scripture speaks strongly about wages. “You shall not oppress a hired worker who is poor and needy… You shall give him his wages on the same day, before the sun sets” (Deuteronomy 24:14–15). James warns rich landowners, “Behold, the wages of the laborers who mowed your fields, which you kept back by fraud, are crying out against you” (James 5:4). So pay on time, pay what you promised, and pay what is fair, not merely the least the market allows. Where you can, share the rewards of success with those who made it possible.

A good culture

A workplace culture is shaped by what the leader rewards, tolerates and models. Do not tolerate bullying, harassment, crude humour or dishonesty, even from star performers. Praise good work specifically. Tell people the truth about how they are doing. Create a place where people can admit mistakes without fear. Boaz greeted his reapers with “The LORD be with you!” and they replied, “The LORD bless you” (Ruth 2:4). The tone of that field was set by its owner.

Hiring

Hire for character as well as competence. Treat applicants fairly and honestly, and do not discriminate on grounds Scripture would not recognise. Should a Christian business hire only Christians? For most roles, no. You are serving the wider world, and the law in many countries forbids it. Faith may properly matter in a few roles directly linked to a Christian mission. But a Christian owner can bless unbelievers greatly simply by giving them a good job and a good boss.

Faith at work

Do not pressure employees to share your faith or attend religious events. That abuses your power, and it does not produce true faith. But you need not hide your faith either. Let your conduct speak first. Be ready to answer when asked (1 Peter 3:15). Offer prayer when someone shares a burden, if they welcome it. Many Christian leaders have found that a reputation for kindness and fairness opens more doors than any programme.

Overwork and safety

Do not make your people pay for your ambition with their health or family life. Plan workloads that are sustainable. Take safety seriously: in Israel, a man building a house had to put a parapet on the roof “that you may not bring the guilt of blood upon your house” (Deuteronomy 22:8). The principle applies to scaffolding, machinery and mental health alike.

Discipline and letting go

Sometimes you must correct or dismiss someone. Do it honestly, early and privately. Do not let problems fester because you dislike conflict; that is unkind to the person and to the team. When you must let someone go, be truthful about the reasons, treat them with dignity, follow the law, and be as generous as you reasonably can. People remember how you treated them on their last day.

A Tuesday afternoon

A warehouse worker’s child is seriously ill. Under the rules, he has used up his leave. His manager, a Christian, finds a way to give him paid time off and covers some of his shifts himself. It costs the firm a little. The worker never forgets it, and neither do his colleagues.

For reflection

If your employees described you to their families, what would they say? Is there anyone you need to treat more justly or kindly?

4.title: Customers
4.essay:
The customer is not king, but the customer is your neighbour. A Christian business serves its customers honestly, sells them what is good for them, and keeps its promises.

Honest weights

The Law forbade cheating in trade: “You shall do no wrong in judgment, in measures of length or weight or quantity. You shall have just balances, just weights” (Leviticus 19:35–36). “A false balance is an abomination to the LORD, but a just weight is his delight” (Proverbs 11:1). Today’s equivalents include hidden charges, misleading labels, shrinking packages at the same price, and software designed to trap people into subscriptions. God sees all of these.

Truthful marketing

Marketing is not wrong. It tells people about something that can help them. But it is easily dishonest. Do not exaggerate, invent urgency, hide the small print, or play on people’s fears and lusts. “Lying lips are an abomination to the LORD, but those who act faithfully are his delight” (Proverbs 12:22). Ask: would I be happy for my customer to see exactly how we decided on this message?

Good products

Make things that are good, not just things that sell. Some products harm people: pornography, predatory loans, gambling designed to hook the vulnerable, apps built to be addictive. A Christian should not make money from these. Even in ordinary businesses, there are choices about quality. Do not cut corners where the customer cannot see them. The craftsman who builds the back of the cabinet as carefully as the front is honouring God.

Fair prices

Prices are set by many things, and a business must make a profit. But it is wrong to exploit people in desperate need. Amos condemned traders who were eager “that we may make the ephah small and the shekel great and deal deceitfully with false balances” (Amos 8:5). Raising prices sharply on essentials after a disaster, or charging the vulnerable more because they do not understand, is not wise business but oppression.

Keeping promises

Deliver what you promised, when you promised. If you cannot, say so early and honestly. Honour warranties and guarantees without making customers fight. The godly person “swears to his own hurt and does not change” (Psalm 15:4): when a promise turns out to be costly, he keeps it anyway.

Complaints and mistakes

Every business makes mistakes. How you handle them shows your character. Listen to complaints without defensiveness. Apologise plainly. Put things right, and a little more. Customers often become most loyal after a problem has been handled well.

A Tuesday afternoon

A garage owner finds that a customer’s car needs only a cheap repair, though she came in expecting a large bill. He could easily charge for more. Instead he tells her the truth and charges for what was done. She tells her friends. Ten years later, half his customers come from people like her.

For reflection

Are there practices in your business, perhaps common in your industry, that would not survive the test of “a just weight is his delight”?

5.title: Suppliers and Partners
5.essay:
Suppliers are often the forgotten neighbours of a business. Large companies especially have great power over them. The Christian leader uses that power justly, pays on time, keeps contracts, and cares about what happens further down the chain.

Paying on time

“Do not withhold good from those to whom it is due, when it is in your power to do it. Do not say to your neighbor, ‘Go, and come again, tomorrow I will give it’—when you have it with you” (Proverbs 3:27–28). Many large firms deliberately pay small suppliers late, using their money as a free loan. For a small supplier, that can mean cash-flow crisis, layoffs or bankruptcy. Paying on time is one of the simplest acts of justice a business can do.

Fair dealing

Negotiate firmly, but not ruthlessly. It is right to seek a good price; it is wrong to squeeze a supplier until they cannot pay their own workers, or to use your size to change terms after the work is done. The golden rule applies: “whatever you wish that others would do to you, do also to them” (Matthew 7:12). Long, trusting relationships with suppliers are usually better business as well as better ethics.

Contracts and your word

Read contracts carefully and keep them. Do not look for loopholes to escape obligations you freely accepted. Jesus said, “Let what you say be simply ‘Yes’ or ‘No’” (Matthew 5:37). A Christian’s handshake should be as good as a signature, though wisdom will still put things in writing.

Bribes and kickbacks

In some countries and industries, bribes are routine. Scripture is clear: “you shall take no bribe, for a bribe blinds the clear-sighted and subverts the cause of those who are in the right” (Exodus 23:8). Refuse to give or take them, even if it costs business. There is a difference between a bribe and a small facilitation payment demanded by an official, and Christians in hard places have thought carefully about where the lines lie. But never pay to have someone betray their duty, and never accept gifts that put you in a supplier’s debt.

The supply chain

Who made your products, and under what conditions? Modern slavery, child labour and dangerous factories are hidden in many global supply chains. A Christian business cannot know everything, but it must not look away. Ask questions, visit where you can, choose suppliers who treat workers decently, and be willing to pay a little more. “Open your mouth for the mute, for the rights of all who are destitute” (Proverbs 31:8).

Partnerships with unbelievers

Paul wrote, “Do not be unequally yoked with unbelievers” (2 Corinthians 6:14). Some Christians take this to forbid any business partnership with a non-Christian. Most Reformed teachers have read it more narrowly: the context is idolatry and spiritual fellowship, so it applies clearly to marriage and church life, but not to every contract. Paul himself expected Christians to deal with unbelievers in the world (1 Corinthians 5:10).

Yet the principle still calls for wisdom. A close, long-term partnership, where you share ownership and decisions, binds you deeply. If your partner does not share your values, you may be pulled into choices you cannot make with a clear conscience. Before entering one, agree in writing on the ethical lines you will not cross.

A Tuesday afternoon

A finance director notices that her company routinely pays small suppliers at ninety days, though the contracts say thirty. It is the industry norm, and it helps the cash flow. She persuades the board to change the policy. A family bakery that supplies the canteen writes to say it saved them from laying off two staff.

For reflection

Is there a supplier or partner who would say you have used your power over them unjustly?

6.title: Competitors, Government and Money
6.essay:
A business lives among competitors, under governments and with money flowing in and out. In each area the Christian leader has to decide whether to follow the market’s rules alone, or the higher rule of love and justice.

Competitors

Competition can be good. It drives quality up and prices down, and it serves customers. But compete by being better, not by lying about rivals, stealing their secrets or poaching their staff by deception. “You shall not bear false witness against your neighbor” (Exodus 20:16), and your competitor is your neighbour. Speak fairly of them, rejoice when they do good work, and help them in trouble if you can.

The law and taxes

Christians are to obey the governing authorities, which are instituted by God (Romans 13:1). That includes employment law, safety rules, environmental standards and tax. “Pay to all what is owed to them: taxes to whom taxes are owed, revenue to whom revenue is owed” (Romans 13:7). Arranging your affairs efficiently within the law is not wrong. But elaborate schemes whose only purpose is to dodge the spirit of the law are hard to square with a clear conscience. The only exception to obeying the law is when it commands you to sin: “We must obey God rather than men” (Acts 5:29).

Debt

“The borrower is the slave of the lender” (Proverbs 22:7). Debt is not forbidden, and many good businesses rightly borrow to grow. But debt brings risk and pressure, and it can tempt leaders into compromises to keep the lenders happy. Borrow cautiously, with a realistic plan to repay. “The wicked borrows but does not pay back” (Psalm 37:21).

Growth and greed

Growth is not always good. Sometimes a business grows so fast that it loses its character, overworks its people or takes on risks that endanger everyone. Jesus warned, “Take care, and be on your guard against all covetousness, for one’s life does not consist in the abundance of his possessions” (Luke 12:15). Ask what the growth is for. More jobs and better service are good reasons; more status for you is not.

Generosity

Profit gives the opportunity to give. Paul tells the rich “to do good, to be rich in good works, to be generous and ready to share” (1 Timothy 6:18). Some Christian business leaders have set a cap on their own income and given away the rest. Others have built foundations or funded missions. Generosity also includes the business itself: sharing profits with staff, supporting the local community, and giving time and skill.

Sunday trading

Should a Christian business open on Sunday? Christians disagree. Some, holding a strict view of the Lord’s Day, close and treat it as a public testimony. Others, believing the Sabbath command is fulfilled in Christ and that the principle is regular rest and worship, open but give staff time off and freedom to attend church. Whichever view you hold, make sure your employees have real rest and opportunity to worship, and respect the convictions of Christian staff who do not want to work on Sundays.

A Tuesday afternoon

A business owner’s accountant shows him a legal scheme to move profits overseas and pay almost no tax. He asks himself whether it fits the spirit of “pay to all what is owed.” He decides it does not. He pays his tax, and also increases his giving.

For reflection

What is your business’s profit for? Write down three purposes you would be glad to explain to God.

7.title: Hard Decisions, Failure and Success
7.essay:
Leaders face decisions with no easy answer, seasons of failure that test their faith, and seasons of success that test it even more. In each, the Christian leader finds wisdom and stability in God.

Hard decisions

Sometimes every option hurts someone. Should you close a loss-making branch, cutting jobs, to save the rest of the company? Should you accept a large contract from a client whose values you doubt? There is often no verse that settles it. Pray for wisdom: “If any of you lacks wisdom, let him ask God, who gives generously to all without reproach, and it will be given him” (James 1:5). Gather the facts, seek counsel, consider everyone affected, decide, and then act with as much honesty and kindness as possible.

Redundancies

If you must cut jobs, do it as a last resort, not first. Look at your own pay and that of senior staff before others. Tell people the truth early, give them as much notice and support as you can, and help them find new work. Remember that behind each name is a family.

Joseph

Joseph ran the economy of Egypt through seven years of plenty and seven years of famine. He planned ahead, stored wisely and fed the nations (Genesis 41:47–57). He was a Hebrew serving a pagan government, yet he kept his integrity. And he could see God’s hand in his story: “As for you, you meant evil against me, but God meant it for good” (Genesis 50:20). The Christian leader likewise plans carefully but trusts God’s providence.

Failure

Many businesses fail, often through no moral fault of the owner. The market changes, a large customer goes under, or a plan simply does not work. Failure is painful, and it can feel like a loss of identity. But your worth does not rest on your company. You are a child of God, and he does not love you less when your business fails. If failure leaves debts, deal with creditors honestly and do what you can to repay. Then learn, grieve and begin again. “The steps of a man are established by the LORD… though he fall, he shall not be cast headlong, for the LORD upholds his hand” (Psalm 37:23–24).

Success

Success is in some ways more dangerous than failure. Moses warned Israel about the time when they would be prosperous: “Beware lest you say in your heart, ‘My power and the might of my hand have gotten me this wealth’” (Deuteronomy 8:17). Successful leaders are tempted to pride, to think their judgment is always right, and to forget God. Stay accountable, keep giving, and keep remembering where it all came from.

Finishing well

Plan for the day when you hand on the business. Train others, share responsibility, and do not hold on too long. Think about what kind of company you want to leave behind: not just a balance sheet, but a culture of honesty, fairness and service. And remember that one day you will hand everything back to God. The question then will not be how large your company became, but whether you were faithful.

The final audit

Every business leader is used to audits. There is one more to come. “For we must all appear before the judgment seat of Christ” (2 Corinthians 5:10). For those in Christ, it is not a judgment that condemns, for that was borne at the cross. But it is a real review of how we used what he gave us. To hear, “Well done, good and faithful servant” (Matthew 25:21) will be worth more than every success the market could give.

For reflection

Are you more anxious about failure or more endangered by success? Bring both to the Lord who gives and takes away.
